Prevention of NTD
Nutritional considerations
Although the terms “folic acid” and “folate” are often used interchangeably, correctly speaking, folic acid refers to the synthetic form
of the vitamin, while folate refers to the natural vitamin forms as found in plant and animal tissues and thus in food sources. The
richest food sources are green leafy vegetables, asparagus, beans, legumes, liver and yeast. Folic acid is found in the human diet only
in fortiﬁed foods and vitamin supplements but is readily converted to the natural cofactor forms of folate after its ingestion. There
are however differences in the chemical structures between folic acid and the natural folate forms and these have important nutri-
tion consequences. Folic acid is a fully oxidized molecule and is a monoglutamate, meaning that it contains just one glutamate
moiety in its structure. Naturally occurring food folates, on the other hand, are a mixture of reduced folate forms (predominantly
5-methylTHF) and typically found as polyglutamates, containing a variable number of glutamate residues. As reduced molecules,
